body.name: Garden Gloves
body.h1: Garden Gloves Dot to Dot — Free 54-Dot Starter Sheet
body.tagline: Ready for a Little Garden Adventure!
body.description: Connect 54 dots to reveal a pair of garden gloves. This easy printable puzzle helps young learners practise number sequencing, pencil control, and concentration.
body.fun_fact: Garden gloves help protect hands from scratches, dirt, and prickly plants while working in the soil.

dot_guide.intro: Every gardener needs a good pair of gloves before they touch the soil, and this 54-dot puzzle draws a matching set — one for each hand. It's a short, friendly puzzle split into four sections, easy to finish in one sitting. Work through the left glove, then the right, then the cuffs that tie them together. Find dot 1 at the fingertip and let's get these hands covered.
dot_guide.outro: Great job — your garden gloves are ready for work! Colour them in your favourite pattern, or keep them classic green and brown like the real thing. Ready to dig a little deeper? Try our dot to dot printables for even more free puzzles.

sections.title: The Left Glove
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 14 to draw the outline of the left glove, including the fingers. Little fingers are tricky, short shapes, so encourage careful, unhurried strokes rather than one quick sweep.
sections.fact: Gardening gloves are usually made with a snug fit around the fingers so a gardener can still pick up small seeds or pull thin weeds without the glove getting in the way.

sections.title: The Right Glove
sections.learn: Continue from dot 15 to dot 27 to draw the matching right glove. Since it mirrors the first one, this section is a good chance to compare the two shapes and check they line up before moving on.
sections.fact: Most gardening gloves are made from a mix of cotton or nylon with a rubber or latex coating on the palm and fingers. The coating helps grip tools and stops water and dirt from soaking straight through.

sections.title: The Cuffs
sections.learn: Trace dots 28 through 41 to add the wide cuffs at the base of each glove. These cuffs flare out a little wider than the rest of the glove, so take it slow around the curve.
sections.fact: Wide cuffs on gardening gloves aren't just for looks — they stop dirt, thorns, and crawling insects from getting inside while a gardener is digging or pruning.

sections.title: The Finishing Stitching
sections.learn: Finish by connecting dots 42 through 54 to add the seam lines and final details across both gloves. Thirteen dots left — a steady, careful finish here really makes the gloves look complete.
sections.fact: Reinforced stitching along the fingers and palm is what makes a good pair of gardening gloves last through a whole growing season instead of wearing through after a few weeks of digging.

body.name: Garden Trowel
body.h1: Garden Trowel Dot to Dot: Just 39 Dots, Free PDF
body.tagline: Dig Into a Little Garden Fun!
body.description: Connect 39 dots to reveal a handy garden trowel. This easy printable puzzle helps young learners practise number sequencing, pencil control, and concentration.
body.fun_fact: A trowel is a small hand tool used for planting seedlings, digging little holes, and moving soil.

dot_guide.intro: A trowel is one of the simplest tools in the garden shed, and this 39-dot puzzle keeps things just as simple — three short sections and a shape kids will recognise right away. Start with the scooped blade, then the neck that connects it to the handle, then the handle itself. Find dot 1 at the tip of the blade and let's start digging.
dot_guide.outro: Nicely done — your trowel is ready to dig! Colour the blade a shiny metal grey and give the handle a bright colour of your choice. If you enjoyed this one, hop over to our dinosaur dot to dot printable collection for a completely different kind of dig.

sections.title: The Blade
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 13 to draw the scooped, pointed blade of the trowel. The curve along one edge is the trickiest part here, so encourage a slow hand rather than a fast, straight line.
sections.fact: A trowel blade is curved rather than flat so it can scoop soil out of a hole in one motion, instead of needing several separate digging and lifting movements like a flat tool would.

sections.title: The Neck
sections.learn: Continue from dot 14 to dot 26 to draw the narrow neck where the blade meets the handle. This is the thinnest part of the whole tool, so keep the lines close together and controlled.
sections.fact: The neck of a trowel is usually the strongest part of the whole tool, since all the pushing and levering force from digging passes right through that narrow section.

sections.title: The Handle
sections.learn: Finish by connecting dots 27 through 39 to draw the rounded handle a gardener grips while digging. Just thirteen dots left — a firm, confident finish here completes the tool.
sections.fact: Trowel handles are often shaped a little wider at the end so the tool doesn't slip out of a gardener's hand, especially when their palms get damp from working in wet soil.

body.name: Wheelbarrow Playground
body.h1: Wheelbarrow Dot to Dot Printable — 85 Dots to Trace
body.description: Connect 85 dots to reveal a sturdy garden wheelbarrow. This mid-level puzzle is great practice for kids who've mastered the easier sheets and are ready for a longer, more detailed picture.
body.fun_fact: The wheelbarrow was invented in ancient China over 2,000 years ago. Early versions could carry several people at once and were even used to move soldiers during wartime.

dot_guide.intro: Eighty-five dots and four sections make up this garden wheelbarrow puzzle. It's a step up from the simplest garden sheets but still an easy one to finish in a single sitting. Work through the wheel first, then the tray, the frame and legs, and finally the handles. Find dot 1 at the front of the wheel and let's get rolling.
dot_guide.outro: That's one loaded-up wheelbarrow, ready for the garden! Colour the tray dirt-brown or paint it bright red like a classic barrow, then pile on some flowers or vegetables of your own design. Ready for something bigger? Try our slide playground puzzle next.

sections.title: The Wheel
sections.learn: Start at dot 1 and connect through to dot 21 to draw the round wheel at the front of the barrow. Circular shapes take a bit more care than straight lines, so encourage slow, even strokes as the curve comes together.
sections.fact: A single wheel at the front lets a wheelbarrow pivot easily in tight spaces, which is exactly why gardeners still prefer this design over a two-wheeled cart for moving soil and plants around flower beds.

sections.title: The Tray
sections.learn: Continue from dot 22 to dot 43 to shape the wide, sloped tray that holds everything the barrow carries. The tray's angled sides are what keep it from tipping loose, so trace them carefully to capture that lean.
sections.fact: The tray on most wheelbarrows tapers narrower at the front and wider at the back. That shape keeps a heavy, lopsided load from sliding forward and spilling out over the wheel.

sections.title: The Frame and Legs
sections.learn: Work from dot 44 to dot 64 to build the frame underneath the tray and the two legs that prop it up when it's resting. These lines are straighter and steadier, a nice change of pace after the curved tray section.
sections.fact: The two legs at the back of a wheelbarrow only touch the ground when it's parked. Lift the handles, and all the weight shifts forward onto the single wheel, which is what makes a full load so much easier to push.

sections.title: The Handles
sections.learn: Finish by connecting dots 65 through 85 to draw the two handles a gardener grips to steer and lift the load. Twenty-one dots left on the last stretch — keep the lines even and finish strong.
sections.fact: Long handles work like a lever. They let one person lift and balance a load that would otherwise be too heavy or awkward to carry by hand, which is the whole trick behind how a wheelbarrow works.
